subject: Your Chase package could not be delivered

message.subject: Your Chase package could not be delivered

findings.title: Sender domain imitates a known domain
evidence: Sender domain chase-account[.]example wraps the name from chase[.]com in extra words (imitating Chase)
findings.lesson: Read the domain letter by letter. Attackers register names that look right at a glance.

findings.title: Link text shows one site, link goes to another
evidence: Link reads "Track your parcel at chase[.]com" but goes to 203[.]0[.]113[.]16
findings.lesson: What a link says and where it goes can differ. Hover to see the real destination before clicking.

findings.title: Sender failed DMARC
evidence: DMARC failed for chase-account[.]example (domain policy: reject)
findings.lesson: A failed sender check means the message may be forged. If it claims to be from someone you know, confirm with them another way.

findings.title: Display name poses as a brand
evidence: Display name "Chase" claims Chase, sent from chase-account[.]example
findings.lesson: The name on a message is free text. Check the address, not just who it says it is.

findings.title: Link goes to a raw IP address
findings.lesson: Real companies use names, not numbers. A link to an IP address is almost never legitimate.

findings.title: Talks as a brand, links nowhere near it
evidence: Opens as Chase but neither the sender nor any link uses a domain that belongs to it
findings.lesson: When a message says it's from a well-known company, go to that company's site yourself instead of using the link.

findings.title: SPF or DKIM check failed
evidence: SPF did not pass for chase-account[.]example
findings.lesson: Real mail from a company is signed. Failed signatures are one more reason to slow down.
